entry.content:
wip: The Cyrillic keys go away when the learner is reading Latin

The row is not a helper beside the keyboard, it IS the keyboard: not one of
the thirty-three letters is on a German, French or Polish one. On the Latin
setting the transcription is written in letters the keyboard already has,
which is the point of it, so the row has nothing to offer and takes up half

the lesson knew Russian at all the row was unreachable.

entry.title: v1.2.1080: The app speaks Russian everywhere except beside a card — u…
entry.content:
v1.2.1080: The app speaks Russian everywhere except beside a card — until now

Russian became a complete interface language in v1.2.1073: every string of the
app, every card note, the pet's voice. The one place it could not follow was
the switch beside a country-course card, which offered German, English, Polish
and French and nothing else. A reader whose whole app was in Russian tapped a
card and got the original back.

Leben in Deutschland is the first course it can read — deliberately the first,
because a Russian speaker sitting the German citizenship test is who that
course is for. All 1,026 of its strings are translated: 628 cards and headings,
407 question strings, the tagline. The other five courses follow, one entry in
the from list each.

Registering a target language is four edits, and three of them fail in silence
if forgotten. check-ru-country-translations demands all four: the table spread
into TRANSLATIONS, the source language present in the from list, "ru" in the
TranslationLanguage union, and — the one that has no symptom until a reader
comes back the next day — getTranslationLanguage accepting a stored "ru", or
the choice is dropped on every reload. Removing that line was tried: the gate
names it exactly.

It also carries the rules the Polish gate learned this week — emphasis that
must survive, keys that must match real course text, tables that may share a
key only when they say the same thing — plus one this course needed: a card
that is nothing but a row of German institution names is allowed to read the
same in both languages, because those names are what has to survive.

entry.title: wip: The lesson learns that Russian is a language
entry.content:
wip: The lesson learns that Russian is a language

Four chains in the lesson asked which language is being taught, and every
one of them had a case for French, Polish, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese
but none for Russian, so a Russian lesson fell through to German. It
labelled Cyrillic as German, tagged the German meaning as English, offered
umlauts to type Russian with, and handed the sentence to a German voice.

Nothing Russian-specific could reach the screen through that: the script
setting never applied, so neither the new transcription line nor the Latin
spelling that shipped long before it ever showed up in a lesson, and the
alphabet badge could not appear at all.

Each chain now names Russian where it already named the others. Proof: the
same lesson rendered under all three script settings used to come out
identical and now differs.

The labels the lesson builds from that name reach every interface table,
Russian included, rather than falling back to English.

entry.title: v1.2.1078: A Polish reader gets the British practice questions too
entry.content:
v1.2.1078: A Polish reader gets the British practice questions too

The Life in the UK course has had a Polish table for its lesson text since
v1.2.1072, but its practice bank had none — so the lesson was read in Polish
and then asked its 248 questions in English. Those questions reach a reader in
three places: folded into the stepped lesson, and through the practice and
test views that all seven country packs share.

1064 strings, keyed on the English of ukQuestionBank.ts exactly as it stands
there, extracted from the built module and paired back by position. Another
251 of the bank's strings were already answered by the course table and are
deliberately absent: every Polish table is spread into one object, so a second
entry for one key would be a silent collision.

Institution and law names stay in English, the way they do in the course
table, because the exam is sat in English and asks for those exact words. A
Polish name appears only where Polish uses nothing else — Tamiza, Londyn,
Kornwalia, Orkady.

check-pl-bank-translation is the new gate. It refuses a key that matches no
real question, a bank string with no Polish anywhere, a key that collides with
another Polish table, and a table nobody spread into the lookup. It also
watches the English names: drop Magna Carta out of the values and it names all
six entries. Both rules were made to fail before this shipped.

Verified in the app, in Polish, on the daily quiz: the question, all four
options and the explanation all come back translated.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: v1.2.1077: Three languages stop writing their dates in English
entry.content:
v1.2.1077: Three languages stop writing their dates in English

Spanish, Italian and Portuguese have been complete interface languages for a
while — every string of the app, every card note. But uiLocale() and
uiSpeechLang() were a chain of ifs ending in a bare English return, and those
three were never added to the chain. An app set to Spanish formatted its dates
and numbers the English way and let the pet speak to its reader in an English
voice, with nothing failing anywhere.

Both helpers now read one table typed on ResolvedInterfaceLanguage, so the next
language cannot be forgotten: a missing row is a type error in the same edit
that adds the language. check-number-formatting no longer names the three tags
it happens to know about — it reads the union and demands a row for every
language in it, and that the row belongs to that language rather than to
another. Dropping Italian was tried: tsc and the gate both refuse it.

Alongside, the Spanish country course finishes its Polish. Four strings were
left out of that table because the gate failed on any key two tables share, and
a year or a one-word heading repeats across courses on its own. The reader saw
Polish regardless, since the tables merge into one lookup — but a card about
Spain was borrowing from tables about Britain and France. The four rows are now
where they belong, with the same wording, and the rule fails only when the two
translations differ, which is the case where one of them is really lost.

One card had also dropped a term the Spanish original prints in bold. Restored,
and the gate counts the markers now: an odd number never closes, and fewer runs
than the source means the card has stopped pointing at something.

entry.title: v1.2.1076: A Polish reader can now open every country course there is
entry.content:
v1.2.1076: A Polish reader can now open every country course there is

Italy, Spain and Russia were the three a Polish reader could not tap
through at all. All three are done — 3053 strings — and with Russia the
last alphabet closes: in front of a Latin sentence you can guess, in
front of Cyrillic you cannot.

Cards, headings and questions in all three. Each country keeps the words
its own counter uses, with the Polish meaning beside them: codice
fiscale and questura, padron and empadronamiento, propiska and dacza.
Names take their Polish form, because a reader who looks one up will
look it up in Polish.

They come in behind the quiz retrofits of v1.2.1072, so the count is
whole rather than partly whole: not one of the 6428 strings across the
seven country courses is left without Polish.

A new gate holds them, modelled on the French one. It compares every
Polish table against every other spread into the same object, since a
shared key loses one translation with no error anywhere, and it asserts
that the picker can actually reach what was written. Its Russian row
carries the pair form: the Cyrillic to find in the key, the
transliteration to require in the value.

Polish now reads seven country courses of seven, the same as German,
English and French.

The gate's Russian row carries the same pair form the French one needed:
the Cyrillic to find in the key, the transliteration to require in the

entry.title: wip: Both Russian alphabets at once, each on its own latch
entry.content:
wip: Both Russian alphabets at once, each on its own latch

The Russian card now carries two independent toggles where English
carries UK and US. Each latches and releases on its own; only the last
one still pressed refuses to release, so a reader is never left with a
card that shows nothing.

With both pressed, every Russian line renders Cyrillic on top and the
transcription as a smaller second line beneath it -- word cards,
dialogue lines and sentences alike. Grading accepts either spelling.

The English row is untouched: it stays mutually exclusive, and none of
its four checks moved.

entry.title: v1.2.1074: Two German cakes were given the names of two other things
entry.content:
v1.2.1074: Two German cakes were given the names of two other things

A native speaker read the counter line and said the German was right and
the English was not. Both halves of it were wrong.

Apfelstreusel is a cake: a base, a layer of apple, streusel on top,
eaten cold with coffee. An apple crumble is a hot pudding with custard
and no base at all — a different dish, not a translation. And
Schwarzwälder on its own is a place in English; it is short for
Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte, which English calls a Black Forest gateau,
as another card in this very course already says. The line now names
both, and carries the shortening as the lesson: a counter drops the
second half of the name and so does the sentence.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: v1.2.1073: The whole app speaks Russian, not only the courses
entry.content:
v1.2.1073: The whole app speaks Russian, not only the courses

Russian was something you could study and nothing more. Every button, every
setting and every card note stayed English while you studied it. It is now an
interface language like the other six.

The two tables it needed:

- i18nRu.ts, 3070 interface strings, the same set the coverage gate demands of
  German, French, Polish, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.
- usageNotesRu.ts, all 14019 card notes, keyed exactly as the other six are.

Registered everywhere a language has to be: the picker list and both resolved
types, the two lazy loaders, the number and speech locales, and the three gates
that would otherwise never look at it.

Two things found on the way there:

- The interface gate was already failing before any of this. One string
  reaches the Spanish, Italian and Portuguese tables and was in none of them,
  so no build could pass at all. Added.
- The 365 daily lines had no Russian, and the type had no room for one. They
  have both now.

uiLocale and uiSpeechLang still answer English for Spanish, Italian and
Portuguese. That gap is older than this and is left where it is.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: v1.2.1072: The four courses a Polish reader opens are whole
entry.content:
v1.2.1072: The four courses a Polish reader opens are whole

The lesson text was already Polish in Life in the UK, Leben in
Deutschland and Vivre en France. The questions that close each lesson
were not, so a reader got through a whole lesson and then met three
untranslated ones. 1069 strings, and none of the 3225 across the three
courses is left without Polish now.

Each course's own words survive. The exam asks for them by name, and an
answer translated away is the wrong answer at the test centre.

Six strings sit in a sibling table rather than being repeated, because
every table for one target is spread into a single object and a second
entry for one key is a silent collision. So the extraction was run again
after each course landed, which is what turned seven such keys up.

A gate had to be corrected on the way. The check that keeps a language
course out of the startup download recognised Polish by the bare word
przynajmniej, an everyday adverb, so an ordinary quiz answer using it
was accused of dragging the whole Polish course into the entry chunk.
Nothing had leaked. The needle is now a full learner sentence that only
the language course can hold, and it still fails the build when that
chunk really is reachable.

entry.title: v1.2.1071: A French reader can now open every country course there is
entry.content:
v1.2.1071: A French reader can now open every country course there is

Poland, Italy, Spain and Russia were the four a French reader could not
tap through. All four are done, and with Russia the last alphabet closes:
in front of a Latin sentence you can guess, in front of Cyrillic you
cannot, so that was the one where the gap actually stopped somebody.

Cards, headings and questions in all four, including the quizzes. A
lesson that ends in three untranslated questions is not a lesson anybody
can finish.

The gate that guards them learned two things on the way. A repeated key
across two tables is silent — the later one wins and a translation is
gone — so every table spread into the same object is now compared with
every other. And an exam word given in Cyrillic can be required in the
key and its transliteration required in the French, which is the only
way to keep the word the country uses in a sentence that has no Cyrillic
left in it.

French now reads seven country courses of seven, the same as German.
